candidates.title: these spinning circles are drawing a dotted sixteenth note 🎵
candidates.description: The outline of a dotted sixteenth note, sampled at 2048 points, is a sum of spinning circles: z(t) = ∑ cₖ eⁱᵏᵗ, with the cₖ from its discrete Fourier transform. Circle k has radius |cₖ| and turns k times per lap. Keep only the N biggest circles and the widest gap to the outline is 27.9% of the symbol's height at N = 2, 9.0% at N = 8, 2.7% at N = 32, 0.58% at N = 128 and 0.14% at N = 512. The dot is a separate shape, so the circles draw the note as one continuous line and hop across to the dot and back: the short straight stroke near the notehead is that hop. The sound is built the same way: an A that gains overtones every time more circles join, with more plucked notes each stage. You asked for a dotted sixteenth (and a semiquaver) in the comments, so here it is. candidates.title: Why 0.999... Is Mathematically Equal to 1
candidates.description: 0.999... is not "almost 1" — it is literally another way of writing the exact number 1. This 10-second visual explainer breaks down why the repeating decimal 0.999... equals 1 using a single 1×1 unit square and four classic mathematical proofs: The Fraction Proof: 1/3 = 0.333..., so multiplying both sides by 3 gives 3/3 = 0.999... = 1. The Algebraic Proof: Setting x = 0.999... and subtracting it from 10x = 9.999... leaves 9x = 9, so x = 1. The Infinite Geometric Series: Adding 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... fills the entire unit square with zero leftover space. The Number Line: Between any two distinct real numbers, you can always fit another number. Because 1 − 0.999... = 0, no number exists between them. Key insight: Our intuition trips up because we expect every real number to have only one decimal representation. In reality, any terminating decimal (like 1 or 0.5) can also be written as an infinite repeating 9s decimal (0.999... or 0.4999...). Save this Short as a quick reference for calculus, real analysis, or the next time this math debate comes up. #Mathematics #0999Equals1 #MathExplained

candidates.title: Riemann Sum vs Integration Explained Visually | Area Under the Sine Curve #riemann #integration
candidates.description: Explore the beautiful connection between Riemann sums and definite integration through this engaging mathematical visualization of the sine function. This video demonstrates how the concept of summation gradually transforms into the idea of integration by using rectangles to approximate the area under the curve of y = sin(x) from zero to pi. Discover how the Riemann sum method works by dividing the area beneath a continuous curve into smaller rectangular sections. Each rectangle represents an approximate contribution to the total area, and the sum of these individual areas provides an estimate of the definite integral. As the number of rectangles increases, the width of each rectangle decreases, producing a more accurate approximation of the actual area. This mathematical visualization illustrates the fundamental relationship between finite sums, limits, and calculus. Watch how the number of rectangles increases progressively, making the rectangular approximation approach the smooth region beneath the sine curve. The comparison between the numerical Riemann sum and the exact value of the definite integral highlights one of the most important ideas in mathematical analysis. The definite integral of sin(x) over the interval from zero to pi equals 2. This result provides a clear example of how integration calculates the accumulated area under a function and how numerical approximation methods can approach an exact mathematical result. The visualization also introduces the midpoint Riemann sum, a numerical integration technique that uses the midpoint of each subinterval to determine the height of its corresponding rectangle. This video is ideal for students learning calculus, definite integrals, limits, numerical integration, and the mathematical foundations of area calculation. It helps make abstract mathematical concepts more intuitive by connecting graphical representations with numerical approximations and analytical results. Key mathematical concepts explored in this video include Riemann sums, definite integration, the sine function, area under a curve, midpoint approximation, limits, continuous functions, and the relationship between summation and integration. These concepts form an essential foundation for advanced calculus, mathematical modeling, physics, engineering, numerical analysis, and other scientific applications. For students preparing for mathematics examinations, competitive exams, or higher-level calculus courses, this visual explanation offers an accessible way to understand how integration emerges from the process of adding increasingly smaller contributions. candidates.title: What is Emotional intelligence ! #divyajain #podcast #shorts
candidates.description: What is Emotional intelligence is a question about how well we understand and manage emotions—both our own and those of other people. In psychology, emotional intelligence involves recognizing emotions accurately, understanding emotional information, using it to support thinking, and regulating emotions effectively. Emotional intelligence can influence the way we communicate, handle conflicts, build relationships and respond to difficult situations. Important aspects include self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social awareness. It does not mean suppressing emotions or never getting angry, sad or anxious; instead, it involves recognizing what you are feeling and responding thoughtfully rather than reacting automatically. This video explores what emotional intelligence really means, how EQ differs from IQ, why understanding emotions matters in personal and professional life, and how emotional awareness can improve communication, decision-making and relationships. The discussion also looks at practical ways to develop better emotional skills in everyday situations.

candidates.title: You Have NEVER Actually Touched Anything! 🤯⚛️ #QuantumPhysics #ScientificFacts #SciFlo #science
candidates.description: Have you ever wondered if you have REALLY touched anything in your entire life? 🤯 According to quantum physics, the reality of touch is far stranger than you might imagine! When you touch another person, hold your phone, or place your hand against a wall, the atoms in your body don’t simply collide like tiny solid objects. Instead, something fascinating happens at the atomic level. ⚛️ THE SCIENCE BEHIND TOUCH 1. Atoms: Everything around you, including your body, is made of atoms. 2. Electrons: Atoms contain negatively charged electrons surrounding their nuclei. 3. Electromagnetic Repulsion: When atoms approach one another, electromagnetic interactions between their electrons strongly resist further compression. 4. Pauli Exclusion Principle: This quantum mechanical principle also helps prevent electrons from occupying identical quantum states. 5. The Sensation of Touch: Your nervous system detects forces and pressure through specialized receptors in your skin, allowing your brain to experience the sensation of touching something. 6. The Quantum Reality: What feels like physical contact is actually the result of complex electromagnetic and quantum interactions between matter. So, when you shake someone’s hand, touch a wall, or hold your phone, you’re experiencing forces between atoms rather than tiny solid surfaces simply meeting. IMPORTANT SCIENTIFIC FACT: Saying that you never touch anything is a simplified way of describing atomic interactions. It doesn’t mean physical contact is imaginary or that atoms never interact. The microscopic world is much stranger than it appears! 🌌 ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🌍 WELCOME TO SCIFLO! 5 Japanese Phrases for When Something Goes Wrong — and the Numbers to Call
candidates.description: Japan is very safe. These five phrases are the small amount of preparation that stays worth doing anyway. For solo travellers and anyone moving to Japan. Ten seconds of preparation for a situation you will probably never meet. Taught by Saku. ▶ Learn Japanese live, 1-on-1, with a hand-picked teacher: https://kodawari-sensei.com/en?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_content=kt31saku ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🚨 The five やめてください — yamete kudasai — "Stop it!" たすけてください — tasukete kudasai — "Help me!" だいじょうぶです — daijōbu desu — "No, thank you." / "I'm fine." けいさつをよんでください — keisatsu o yonde kudasai — "Call the police." えいごはなせますか？ — eigo hanasemasu ka? — "Do you speak English?" **110** — police · **119** — fire and ambulance. Both free from any phone, including a locked one. **だいじょうぶです is the one you will actually use** — it is how you decline anything in Japan, firmly and without confrontation. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🗾 The small police box on the corner 交番 — こうばん — kōban — a neighbourhood police box 交 — こう — kō — exchange, alternate 番 — ばん — ban — a turn, a watch, a number Literally "alternating watch" — officers took shifts. **There are over 6,000 of them across Japan**, usually a small building at a busy intersection with a red lamp outside, staffed around the clock. **And it is the single most useful thing to know about being lost in Japan.** A 交番 is not a police station — it is closer to a permanently staffed help desk that happens to be police. Officers there will: - give you directions, with a map, at any hour - take lost property. **Japan's lost-and-found rate is genuinely remarkable** and it runs through 交番. - lend you the train fare home in some cases 落とし物 — おとしもの — otoshimono — a lost item 忘れ物 — わすれもの — wasuremono — something left behind 交番はどこですか — kōban wa doko desu ka — where's the police box? **If you lose something on a train**, it goes to the station office first and then to a central lost property centre. Report it — the recovery rate for phones and wallets in Japan is high enough that it is worth the twenty minutes. The bigger buildings: 警察署 — けいさつしょ — keisatsusho — a full police station 派出所 — はしゅつじょ — hashutsujo — the older word for 交番, still on some signs And 番 turns up all over: 交番, 一番 (ichiban, number one), 番号 (bangō, a number), 当番 (tōban, being on duty). 🔎 emergency Japanese phrases, koban police box Japan, 110 119 Japan, lost something in Japan, otoshimono, yamete kudasai, solo travel Japan safety. #Shorts #LearnJapanese #Japanese #JapanTravel #JapanSafety

candidates.description: The first use of the idea of ‘sine’ in the way we use it today was in the work Aryabhatiyam by Aryabhata, in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word ardha-jya for the half-chord, which was shortened to jya or jiva in due course. When the Aryabhatiyam was translated into Arabic, the word jiva was retained as it is. The word jiva was translated into sinus, which means curve, when the Arabic version was translated into Latin. Soon the word sinus, also used as sine, became common in mathematical texts throughout Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund Gunter (1581–1626), first used the abbreviated notation ‘sin’. The origin of the terms ‘cosine’ and ‘tangent’ was much later. The cosine function arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta called it kotijya. The name cosinus originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation ‘cos’.

candidates.title: Here's a neuroscience trick for when someone annoys you
candidates.description: Here's a neuroscience trick for when someone annoys you. Nobody can make you annoyed, the energy is in you. And that is good news. Follow me, then comment UPSPIRAL and I'll send you some more information about my brand new manifestation program, the Up Spiral Lab. You can also click the link in my bio. Every time you indulge annoyance, you train your brain to get annoyed faster. Neuroplasticity 101. You build new neural connections that reinforce annoyance. Flip it with this 4-step hack. One. Hand on heart. This activates oxytocin and flips your body out of fight mode. An instant free chemistry flip. Two. Smile. Yes, even a fake smile. Smiling lights up the brain's reward circuits and dials down stress chemistry. Your nervous system cannot stay fully annoyed when your face insists on joy. Three. Zoom out. Will this matter in 10 minutes? What about 10 days? What about 10 years? Will it matter on your last day on Earth? No? Then stop renting it space in your head. Four. Appreciate. Find three things to appreciate about the other person, however small. Appreciation scrambles the annoyance pattern completely. Try staying annoyed while you are busy noticing what is good. It does not work. An annoyance is basically a free gym membership for building patience. And patience practiced long enough looks a lot like power.

candidates.title: Why a Paper Cut Hurts More Than a Knife Cut
candidates.description: How does a harmless sheet of paper slice your finger worse than a kitchen knife, when it's made from 99% water and zero glue? 📄🔪 Here's the full journey: giant spinning blades chop a log into wood chips, a pressure tank boils out the brown natural glue (lignin), and the leftover white fibers become a soup that's 99% water. That soup blasts onto a screen moving at 60 mph, the water drains away, and the fibers hook together all on their own. That's why paper is strong when dry but turns to mush in the washing machine. Finally, hot steel rollers press it flat, turning those jagged fibers into a microscopic chainsaw edge. ⚙️ Covered in this Short: • Wood chipper → wood chips • Pressure tank: boiling out the natural glue (lignin) • 99% water pulp • The 60 mph forming screen • Why fibers hook together with no glue (and why receipts turn to mush) • Steam drums + calender rollers • The microscopic "chainsaw" edge behind every paper cut 🔔 Subscribe to OverEngineered Lab for more everyday engineering explained in 3D. #engineering #paper #papercut #howitsmade #manufacturing #3danimation

candidates.title: How Ancient Romans Harvested And Stored Ice In Hot Summers #shorts
candidates.description: ​In 62 AD, across the Italian peninsula and imperial cities—documented by Seneca the Younger in Naturales Quaestiones (Book 4B, Chapter 13 on mountain snow and ice harvesting, straw insulation, and summer ice markets in Rome), Pliny the Elder in Natural History (Book 19, Chapter 19 and Book 31, Chapter 23 on packed snow pits and mountain ice transport), and Martial in Epigrams (Book 14, Epigrams 116–118)—wealthy villas, public baths, and urban wine shops enjoyed crystal-clear ice even in the middle of August. How did ancient Roman crews harvest, haul, and preserve solid mountain ice long before mechanical refrigeration existed? By forging wide-bladed iron ice saws with deep raker teeth, outfitting winter workers with spiked iron traction cleats and hinged lifting tongs, and sealing stacked ice blocks inside deep straw-and-sawdust-insulated subterranean stone pits (nivaria), Rome kept winter ice frozen all summer long. Want to verify the primary historical sources yourself? Look up Seneca the Younger's Naturales Quaestiones Book 4B Chapter 13 on Roman ice and snow storage, Pliny the Elder's Natural History Book 19 Chapter 19, and ancient Roman subterranean nivaria ice pits. candidates.description: Margaret and Frances Macdonald: The Spook School | Glasgow Style, Art Nouveau & Symbolism This is a short of a longer video. Discover the extraordinary art and fascinating lives of Margaret Macdonald and Frances Macdonald, two pioneering female artists who helped shape the Glasgow Style and the Art Nouveau movement at the turn of the 20th century. Often associated with the mysterious Spook School, the Macdonald sisters created some of the most distinctive, dreamlike, and symbolically rich works of modern decorative art. In this art history documentary, we explore the lives, artistic influences, and remarkable contributions of Margaret and Frances Macdonald, members of the legendary Glasgow Four alongside Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Herbert MacNair. Together, they developed a revolutionary visual language combining Art Nouveau design, Symbolism, spirituality, nature, and the Arts and Crafts movement. Learn how the Glasgow School of Art became the center of an artistic revolution, and how the Macdonald sisters transformed traditional ideas about beauty, femininity, and decorative art. Explore their connections to Japanese art and Japonisme, Celtic knotwork, Symbolist painting, and the flowing organic lines of Art Nouveau. We examine the distinctive characteristics of the Glasgow Style, including elongated ethereal figures, flowing hair, mysterious dreamlike compositions, intricate decorative patterns, symbolic flowers, and delicate pastel colors. Their innovative use of watercolor, gouache, gesso, metallic paint, glass beads, and mother-of-pearl created extraordinary textured surfaces that blurred the boundaries between fine art, interior design, and decorative arts. Famous Artworks Explored in This Video Frances Macdonald – A Paradox (1895): An unsettling Symbolist composition exploring duality, mystery, and the themes of life and death. Margaret Macdonald – The May Queen (1900): An exquisite decorative work celebrating spring, renewal, femininity, and nature. Margaret Macdonald – The White Rose and the Red Rose (1902): A symbolic composition exploring romantic love, purity, spirituality, and the beauty of Art Nouveau design. Frances Macdonald – The Choice (c. 1896): A psychologically intense watercolor exploring spiritual choices, temptation, and opposing forces. Discover why the sisters' work initially confused and shocked London critics, earning the nickname the Spook School, while attracting admiration from the Vienna Secession and influential artists such as Gustav Klimt. We also examine how their artistic legacy extended beyond Art Nouveau, influencing modern decorative design, Art Deco, Symbolism, and even later movements exploring dreams, fantasy, and the subconscious, including Surrealism. For many years, the achievements of Margaret and Frances Macdonald were overshadowed by their husbands, Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Herbert MacNair. Today, their work is increasingly recognized for its originality, innovation, and profound contribution to modern art. Explore the fascinating world of the Glasgow Four, Art Nouveau, Symbolism, and the visionary women artists who helped redefine modern art. candidates.title: Why the first second always feels longer #science #neuroscience #explained
candidates.description: Look at a clock with a second hand. That first second always seems to hang there a beat too long. 👁️ Getting your eyes to the clock takes a saccade — a fast jump — and your brain turns the picture down while your eyes are moving. That leaves a gap of missing footage. 🕐 Rather than show you the gap, your brain backdates the first thing you land on and fills the missing interval with it. So the stretched second isn't your imagination: you really were shown that image for longer than a second. ⏱️ It's called chronostasis, and the stretch is small — measurements put it at up to roughly a tenth of a second — but it's reliable enough that you can trigger it on purpose with any clock. 👀 It's also the same suppression that makes it impossible to watch your own eyes move in a mirror. One hides a movement; the other stretches a moment. There's a separate video on this channel about the mirror version. 🔔 Subscribe for more short explainers on why your body does the weird things it does. #science #humanbody #shorts

Behavioral Neuroscience
candidates.description: Cognitive neuroscience studies thoughts. Behavioral neuroscience studies what you actually do. Here is what the research actually says about behavioral neuroscience. It is the biological basis of behaviour, in humans and in animals, and it grew out of what used to be called physiological psychology. Every study has the same skeleton: measure activity somewhere in the nervous system, then set it against one behavioural variable. A perception, a reaction, a decision. The thought in between belongs to the other field. KEY FACTS - Behavioral neuroscience is the study of the biological basis of behavior in humans and animals. - It is the broader, contemporary development of Physiological Psychology and is sometimes called Biological Psychology. - It examines the brain's neurotransmissions and the psychological events associated with biological activity. - Topics span genetic and molecular substrates of behavior, neuropsychology, learning and memory, motivation and emotion, and sensory processes. - The field studies the interplay between the brain, behavior and the environment. - Studies examine what creates, controls and coordinates perception, action, reaction or decision-making. Read the full behavioral neuroscience article: https://www.emotiv.com/blogs/glossary/behavioral-neuroscience EMOTIV translates peer-reviewed neuroscience into short, accurate explainers. No hype. candidates.description: Did you know that humans learned to make bread nearly 4,000 years before the invention of agriculture? candidates.description: An infinite series can converge to a finite sum, even when you keep adding positive numbers forever. By slicing a single square into smaller fractions, we can visualize how adding 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and beyond fills the total area of 1 exactly. This geometric approach shows that as long as each new piece covers only half of the remaining space, the total area will never exceed the boundaries of the original square. Understanding how an infinite series works helps clarify why these sums do not explode to infinity. Seeing the math as a physical shape makes the concept of convergence intuitive, proving that a finite sum is the logical result of this process. candidates.title: How Italy Became One Country, From 7 Pieces to 1 Kingdom 🤯  #geography #animation #history #shorts
candidates.description: In 1859 there was no country called Italy. The peninsula was split into seven pieces: kingdoms, duchies, the Papal States, and Austrian-ruled Lombardy and Venetia. Just twelve years later, Rome was the capital of a united Kingdom of Italy. Here's how it happened: Sardinia teamed up with France in 1859, central Italy voted to join in 1860, Garibaldi's Thousand took the south, the Kingdom of Italy was born on 17 March 1861, Venice followed in 1866, and Rome in 1870. Italy as a state is younger than the USA (1861 vs 1776), but Italian history and culture go back thousands of years. candidates.title: NASA Found a Tiny Moon Hiding in Saturn’s Rings! 😳🪐 #Shorts
candidates.description: Scientists spotted mysterious waves in Saturn’s rings before discovering the tiny moon responsible for them! 😳🪐 Meet Daphnis, one of Saturn’s smallest and most fascinating moons! Approximately 8 kilometers (5 miles) across, Daphnis orbits inside the 42-kilometer-wide Keeler Gap in Saturn’s A ring. But here's what makes this discovery incredible: Before Daphnis was discovered on May 1, 2005, scientists had already suspected a hidden moon was there because of mysterious ripples along the edge of the Keeler Gap! Its gravity creates waves in the surrounding ring particles, sculpting the edges of the gap. These waves extend both horizontally and vertically, creating incredible structures in Saturn’s rings. NASA’s Cassini spacecraft captured its closest-ever view of Daphnis on January 16, 2017. Even a tiny moon can reshape the rings of a giant planet! 🔭 NASA Official Sources: Daphnis – NASA: https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/moons/daphnis/ 🌌 Follow Qunova Labs for fascinating space discoveries, astronomy facts, NASA discoveries and mysteries of our universe. #saturn #daphnis #nasa #saturnrings #space #astronomy #spacefacts #science #spaceexploration #shorts

candidates.title: This sun is no brighter than the sky around it | Impression, Sunrise #art #history
candidates.description: Fine art films for art lovers, museumgoers and anyone who hangs art at home. The short ones find the detail most people miss in a famous painting; the long ones pair paintings with classical music for reading, studying or a quiet evening. Claude Monet painted the harbour of Le Havre at sunrise in 1872, and the picture gave Impressionism its name. The orange sun looks like the brightest thing on the canvas, but when its brightness is measured, it is the same as the grey sky around it. Take the colour away and the sun almost disappears. Harvard neuroscientist Margaret Livingstone explains why it seems to shimmer: the part of our vision that judges position and depth sees only brightness, not colour, so it can't pin the sun down. The painting hangs in the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris. There's a new painting every day, so subscribe if you'd like to keep looking. candidates.title: Why a Coffee Cup and a Donut Are the Same Shape (Topology Explained)
candidates.description: To a mathematician, a coffee cup and a donut are the same shape. ☕🍩 This is topology, the study of properties that stay the same when you stretch, bend, or squeeze an object without tearing or gluing. A mug has one handle-like hole going all the way through it, and so does a donut. Squish the cup’s bowl down, grow the handle, and you get a donut, with no cutting required. Mathematicians say the two are homeomorphic, and both have genus 1. A sphere is different. It has no through-hole, so you can’t turn it into a donut without tearing a hole in it. 🔴 Topology ignores size, thickness, and curvature and focuses on the underlying structure that links seemingly different shapes. In this short, you’ll learn: ✅ What topology studies ✅ What a through-hole and genus are ✅ What homeomorphic means ✅ Why a sphere can’t become a donut without tearing 👍 Like if this changed how you see your coffee cup 💬 Comment: What everyday object would you try next, a pretzel, a pair of glasses, or a bowl? 🔔 Subscribe for more math, physics, and chemistry explained clearly ↗️ Share with someone who loves puzzles or math #Shorts #Topology #Math #Mathematics #Donut #CoffeeCup #Geometry #STEM #MathExplained #ScienceExplained

candidates.title: Why Derivatives and Integrals Connect #math #calculus #shorts
candidates.description: Learn calculus in 30 seconds by mastering the two core concepts that define how we measure change and space. Calculus relies on two fundamental ideas: the derivative and the integral. The derivative calculates instant speed by analyzing the slope of a curve, while the integral determines total area by summing up small, individual slices. Understanding how these inverse operations relate growth to totals is essential for visualizing complex mathematical relationships. Whether you are studying for an exam or building a foundation for higher-level math, grasping these basics clarifies how speed connects to distance. Once you see the link between these two core operations, the mechanics of advanced math become much more intuitive. Which math concepts are you finding tricky right now?
